The unit is held apart from the wisdom proem before it (a shift from third-person maxim to first-person counsel) and from the gnomic time-and-procedure reflection after it (a shift from direct address to third-person generalization at web:Eccl.8.5).

boundary_rationale: A gnomic principle opens this reflection, “וְעֵ֣ת וּמִשְׁפָּ֔ט יֵדַ֖ע לֵ֥ב חָכָֽם” (oshb:Eccl.8.5, byte tier), “his wise heart will know the time and procedure” (web:Eccl.8.5), and the same pairing recurs verbatim, “יֵ֖שׁ עֵ֣ת וּמִשְׁפָּ֑ט” (oshb:Eccl.8.6, byte tier), “there is a time and procedure for every purpose” (web:Eccl.8.6) -- the repeated phrase binds the two verses before the span turns to human powerlessness before fate and death (web:Eccl.8.7-Eccl.8.8: no power over the spirit, no discharge in war). The span closes on the book's own observation frame, “אֶת כָּל זֶ֤ה רָאִ֨יתִי֙ וְנָת֣וֹן אֶת לִבִּ֔י” (oshb:Eccl.8.9, byte tier), “All this I have seen, and applied my mind to every work that is done under the sun” (web:Eccl.8.9), which both caps this reflection and sets up the specific case the next row develops. The span is held apart from the king-conduct admonition before it (address versus generalization) and treated as one unit through its own internal shift from gnomic principle to fate-reflection to observation-frame close, since no verse in between opens a fresh topic or address.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting web:Eccl.8.5-Eccl.8.6 (the repeated time-and-procedure principle) from web:Eccl.8.7-Eccl.8.9 (fate and observation) was considered, but 8:7's own “for” clause depends on 8:6's principle (misery follows from not knowing the time), so the span reads as one connected reflection rather than two.

The span's closing verse opens with the same refrain word, “יֶשׁ הֶבֶל֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נַעֲשָׂ֣ה עַל הָאָרֶץ֒ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יֵ֣שׁ צַדִּיקִ֗ים” (oshb:Eccl.8.14, byte tier), “There is a vanity which is done on the earth” (web:Eccl.8.14), and closes on it again, “אָמַ֕רְתִּי שֶׁגַּם זֶ֖ה הָֽבֶל” (oshb:Eccl.8.14, byte tier), “I said that this also is vanity” (web:Eccl.8.14) -- a hevel bracket opening and closing the paradox (righteous men suffering the wicked's due, wicked men receiving the righteous' due).
